item.title: Coordinated housing and health care models better serve homeless populations
item.description: Organizations aiming to help homeless people with either housing or health care can be more effective when they form partnerships with other service groups, a Rutgers study has found.

item.title: ECG-based AI model doubles early liver disease diagnoses
item.description: As rates of obesity, high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes and sleep apnea increase, cases of advanced chronic liver disease and resulting liver scarring or cirrhosis also are rising. Patients often are diagnosed based on symptoms, such as gastrointestinal bleeding, fluid retention or jaundice, which happen when liver disease has progressed to a late stage.

item.title: AI analysis of chest X-rays may reveal early signs of aging
item.description: Artificial intelligence may be able to reveal how fast your body is aging by analyzing a chest X-ray, according to a new study published in The Journals of Gerontology. Researchers found that a deep learning model was able to detect subtle, age-related changes in the heart, lungs, and overall health more effectively than leading DNA-based "epigenetic clocks."

item.title: Social isolation emerges as a key, independent risk factor for cognitive decline
item.description: Using longitudinal data from the US Health and Retirement Study, this study applied causal inference modeling to disentangle the independent and joint effects of social isolation and loneliness on later-life cognitive function. It shows that reducing social isolation is associated with modest but meaningful protection against cognitive decline, with loneliness mediating only a small proportion of this effect.

item.title: Cannabis use alters sleep stages in people with chronic pain
item.description: The most frequently reported reasons for medicinal cannabis use are for pain relief and improvements in sleep.

item.title: Genetic differences can affect the effectiveness of antibody therapies
item.description: The genome differs from person to person in thousands of positions. In some cases, this means that proteins have a different building block in certain regions, rendering some antibody-based therapies ineffective, report researchers from the University of Basel, Switzerland.

item.title: High-dose rifampicin does not improve survival in tuberculosis meningitis
item.description: Each year, 11 million people worldwide develop tuberculosis, and about 1.4 million die from it. Meningitis occurs in 1–2% of patients and is the most severe complication of tuberculosis, arising when the bacteria reach the brain.

item.title: Study finds small sex differences in recovery after ischemic stroke
item.description: When examining recovery during the first year after an ischemic stroke, a new study has found for daily tasks such as eating, dressing and driving, female participants experienced slightly worse recovery than male participants.

item.title: Eating high-fat cheese and cream may be linked to lower dementia risk
item.description: Eating more high-fat cheese and high-fat cream may be linked to a lower risk of developing dementia, according to a new study published on December 17, 2025, in Neurology, the medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology.

item.title: Many women suffer in silence from treatable pelvic floor conditions
item.description: Many women assume pelvic floor health issues are simply their fate—part of having vaginal deliveries, getting older, gaining weight or entering menopause. Perhaps they have watched their mothers and grandmothers live with symptoms, such as urinary incontinence and pain.
